summary: A DigitalOcean community tutorial by William Imoh, last updated March 19, 2024, explaining four uses of JavaScript's .map() array method. It covers calling a function on each array item, converting a string to an array using Array.prototype.map with .call(), rendering lists in React, and reformatting arrays of objects. The page's navigation, footer and comment boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: Tutorial by William Imoh on four practical uses of JavaScript's .map() method, including string conversion and React list rendering.
key_facts: The tutorial is titled 'How To Use JavaScript Maps - .map()' and was updated on March 19, 2024.
William Imoh is the author of the tutorial.
The .map() method creates a new array by calling a specific function on each item in the parent array.
The article describes .map() as a non-mutating method, as opposed to mutating methods that only change the calling array.
The first use case shows that sweetArray [2, 3, 4, 5, 35] mapped with sweetItem * 2 produces [4, 6, 8, 10, 70].
The second use case uses Array.prototype.map.call on the string 'Sammy' with each letter appended with 'a', producing ["Sa", "aa", "ma", "ma", "ya"].
The tutorial says the string conversion works like the .split() method of a string, except each character can be modified before being returned in an array.
The third use case shows JavaScript libraries like React using .map() inside JSX to render list items, using the names array whale, squid, turtle, coral, starfish.
The React example renders the list into a DOM element with id 'root' using ReactDOM.
The fourth use case reformats an array of objects, producing [{shark: "ocean", age: 50}, {turtle: "pond", age: 60}, {otter: "fish biscuits", age: 50}].
The tutorial's prerequisites note that no coding is required, but readers can follow along with the Node.js REPL or browser developer tools.
The tutorial is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International.
The conclusion points readers to the article 'How To Use Array Methods in JavaScript: Iteration Methods' for more information.
